doc.title: Orrin Keepnews interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Poor sales of the first Evans record and Everybody Digs Bill Evans
summary: The first album sold about 800 copies a year, and the second with Philly Joe and Sam Jones began the quotes cover.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Cannonball Adderley: the sound, the man, the band

blocks.x: capable of being influenced simultaneously by Horace Silver and Lennie Tristano. You try that sometime and you know what you get? You get Bill Evans. And the other fact is that yes, I was tremendously impressed by Bill and the interesting thing about Bill of course was that in an age when then, as is true now I’m quite sure, of course it is, guys will kill to get into the recording studio. Everybody is always ready and more than ready to record. After Bill did that first record which got very, very good critical reaction, which sold practically nothing, it was very hard to get him back in the studio. Now again, one of the things we should not neglect is the strange attitudes of most of us foolish people who were fans transmuted into record companies. We were doing this thing and I don’t think we ever even thought seriously about whether it was a commercially viable thing to be doing. We were in business to make records. And we were very happy to be making records. It was kind of rough perhaps if, as I did, you had a family. Somehow or other I managed to eke out a living. The record company sure didn’t contribute very much to it in the early days. But the fact that Bill Evans made a record that didn’t sell a God damn, that was — let’s put it this way it did not reach in its initial year it did not reach four figures. It didn’t crack a thousand in its first year. Didn’t do that until a year later when he was discovered by Miles. And when he was playing — well initial sales the first year on the first Bill Evans record, 800 copies. But in a revolutionary move, in the second year when he was now known as a sideman with Miles Davis it sold another 800. Now that cumulative total still isn’t much but any record selling as much in the second year as it has in the first, that’s a phenomenon. Bill — I played hell trying to get him back into the studio. Actually what happened was it then, it got to be right after he left Miles, and just prior to the time of his starting what would be his own trio for the rest of his life, he made that second record in which Philly Joe, who he had known from the Miles period, and Sam Jones, who he was very impressed with. It’s kind of interesting, Bill Evans, who a lot of people — whose music a lot of people wrongly confuse with Debussy — being attracted by what was probably the best walking roots bass player that we had in jazz at that time, and that’s a wonderful trio record, which I for some reason was brash enough to come up with the title “Everybody Digs Bill Evans.” And that was the record, the cover of which consists of laudatory quotes from four different people. Well what happened with that was I had read — the Miles quote there is something that had appeared in a Down Beat article, Miles talking about Bill. And that’s when the idea got into my head and I said well it shouldn’t be too difficult. I know that a lot of other piano players feel strongly about him and I know that Cannonball feels strongly about him. Cannonball by that time was working with me. I got a quote from Cannonball just by asking for it.
